name: Bimatoprost
lead: Bimatoprost is a synthetic prostamide, a structural analogue of prostaglandin F2-alpha, applied to the eye or eyelid margin. It is sold as Lumigan and generics for open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension, and as Latisse for eyelash hypotrichosis, a condition of sparse or short lashes [1][2]. The US Food and Drug Administration approved it for glaucoma in 2001 [1].

In appearance communities it is used to lengthen, thicken and darken eyelashes, and some users apply it to eyebrows off-label. Lashes are set mainly by genetics, with upper lashes usually 7 to 8 mm and rarely exceeding 10 mm, and they thin with age, so a product that lengthens and darkens them changes the framing of the eyes without makeup [35]. Randomised trials of the 0.03% solution reported increases in lash length, fullness and darkness over vehicle, and the effect is described as fading after use stops [2][4][5]. Small studies have also examined eyebrow and scalp use, but these are not approved indications [6][7].

The route from a glaucoma drop to a cosmetic product is itself part of the story: lash growth was noticed as a side effect in glaucoma patients, which led to the Latisse approval in December 2008 [2]. Online, the drug is discussed under the names Latisse and Careprost, alongside threads on side effects, eye colour change, access and alternatives [28][30][38][40].

Documented adverse effects include conjunctival redness, itching, darkening of the eyelid skin, and permanent iris darkening; periorbital fat changes have also been reported [3][1][2]. The drug is prescription-only in the United States, and over-the-counter lash serums are regulated as cosmetics rather than drugs [2][8].

paras: Bimatoprost is used in adults with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension, alone or combined with the beta blocker timolol [1][3]. The US label describes it as a prostaglandin analogue indicated to reduce elevated intraocular pressure [9]. Network meta-analyses and head-to-head trials have compared it with timolol, latanoprost and travoprost; Wikipedia summarises these as finding it more effective than timolol and at least as effective as latanoprost and travoprost at lowering pressure [1][10][11][12][13].
A sustained-release intracameral implant has also been approved for glaucoma, with effects lasting about a year, as described in a 2025 review of new glaucoma treatments [14].

The 0.03% solution is approved as Latisse for eyelash hypotrichosis, a condition of inadequate or sparse lashes. Wikipedia notes the approval is for essentially cosmetic purposes [1]. According to Grokipedia, the approval followed observations of lash growth in glaucoma patients, and the label regimen is a nightly application to the upper eyelid margin with a sterile single-use applicator [2].

Off-label uses described in the literature include eyebrow hypotrichosis and scalp hair loss. A 2011 placebo-controlled study of the drug on eyebrows was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov [6], and a pilot randomised trial compared it with mometasone in scalp alopecia areata [7].

Wikipedia's eyelash article notes that each lid can hold up to six rows of lashes, that follicle number cannot increase after birth, that length is set mainly by genetics, and that length, thickness and darkness decline with age [35]. Allergan's Latisse is described there as the first FDA-approved drug for eyelash growth, with visible growth within 16 weeks mostly on the upper lashes and length increases of up to 25 percent [35]. Law's 2010 review describes the labelled approach as one drop on a single-use applicator drawn along the roots of the upper lashes once nightly, with a fresh applicator for each eye [4].

Other ways people enhance lashes include false lashes and extensions, mascara, curlers and perms, lash conditioners, and, in Wikipedia's account, transplants of scalp hair that keep growing like scalp hair and need trimming [35]. Some non-prostaglandin serums use peptides instead because of regulation in Canada and California [35]. Threads on looksmax.org compare Latisse with alternatives and with ways to build lashes without it [38][39].

In the phase III trials summarised by Grokipedia, nightly application for 16 weeks increased lash length by about 25 percent, fullness by about 106 percent and darkness by about 18 percent versus vehicle, with visible change typically from about four weeks and full effect at 12 to 16 weeks [2]. Published reviews of bimatoprost for lash hypotrichosis describe the trial programme and adverse-event rates [15][16]. A 2024 review of eyelash serums concluded that the prostaglandin analogues have the stronger evidence base among lash products, while non-prostaglandin serums vary [8].

Law's 2010 review describes the pivotal programme as a randomised, vehicle-controlled multicentre trial of 278 patients (137 on bimatoprost, 141 on vehicle) using once-nightly application to the upper lid margin for 16 weeks and a four-point Global Eyelash Assessment scale. Improvement of at least one grade was seen in 78 percent of the bimatoprost group versus 18 percent on vehicle, and improvement of at least two grades in 32.8 percent versus 1.4 percent; mean lash length rose by about 1.4 mm (25 percent) versus 0.1 mm (2 percent) [4]. The review reports that iris pigmentation was not seen in the lash trial, which it attributes to the drug staying at the lid margin, and that observable lash growth resolved after stopping latanoprost or bimatoprost [4]. In a separate three-month glaucoma comparison cited there, eyelash growth occurred in 13 percent on bimatoprost versus 4 percent on latanoprost [4].

A 2024 narrative review in Pharmaceuticals (Zeppieri and colleagues) screened 583 PubMed records and considered 425 studies from 2010 to 2023. It reports that hair and lash changes with the 0.03% gel appear within one to two months, that bimatoprost solution and gel improved lash loss after chemotherapy in study groups, and that authors advise using it only after chemotherapy [5]. Its glaucoma tables include a 2005 meta-analysis of 42 studies and 9,295 participants reporting pressure reductions of 30.3 percent for bimatoprost, 28.7 percent for travoprost and 26.7 percent for latanoprost [5].

Eyebrows: a small placebo-controlled study of Latisse for eyebrow hypotrichosis (n=20) was completed in 2011 [6]. A published case report described increased eyebrow hair growth and thickening in a woman after eight months of daily use [1].

Scalp: a pilot randomised study compared bimatoprost with mometasone furoate in scalp alopecia areata [7]. A phase 1 safety and pharmacokinetic study in men with androgenetic alopecia was registered and terminated [17]. Reviews of chemotherapy-induced alopecia list other interventions and do not establish bimatoprost as an approved option [18].

Glaucoma: large randomised trials have compared bimatoprost with timolol, latanoprost and travoprost over 12 weeks to 12 months [10][11][12][13][19]. A network meta-analysis of 114 randomised trials ranked first-line glaucoma medications by pressure reduction [20], and an earlier meta-analysis covered the main drug classes [21].

The most common effect is conjunctival hyperemia (redness), reported in more than 10 percent of patients on the eye-drop formulation, and the US label cites 45 percent for the most common reaction [1][9]. Other reported effects include itching, burning, blurred vision, and eyelash changes [1][9].

The label warns of pigmentation of the iris, periorbital tissue (eyelid) and eyelashes. Iris pigmentation is likely to be permanent, while lash changes are usually reversible [9]. Wikipedia reports that cosmetic-formulation effects include eyelid or under-eye darkening and infection if single-use applicators are reused [1]. Grokipedia additionally lists periorbital fat atrophy and unintended hair growth where the solution contacts skin [2]. Wikipedia reports a study suggesting that blotting excess solution after drop instillation was associated with shorter lashes and less eyelid pigmentation [1].

The label also lists intraocular inflammation, macular edema and hypersensitivity as warnings or contraindications [9]. Regarding pregnancy, the label states there are no adequate controlled studies in pregnant women, and that high oral doses caused abortion and early delivery in mice and rats [9]. Wikipedia states use in pregnancy and breastfeeding is generally not recommended [1].

Periocular changes described in the literature include deepening of the upper eyelid sulcus, prostaglandin-associated periorbitopathy and orbital fat loss, and the 2024 review notes the fat-loss effect has been considered potentially useful in Graves' orbitopathy although one study found it insignificant [5]. Grokipedia reports iris pigmentation changes in about 1 to 3 percent of users, mainly with hazel or green-brown irises, and periorbital skin darkening in about 3 to 10 percent, usually reversible [2]. Wikipedia describes the periorbital effect in terms of skin darkening around the eye [36].

The 2024 review lists reduced corneal endothelial cell density, benzalkonium chloride toxicity and, rarely, cystoid macular edema and retinal or choroidal detachment, mainly in elderly patients with prior eye surgery [5]. Wikipedia notes that wider use of prostaglandin analogues has been limited by side effects and abortive potential [36].

For intraocular pressure, bimatoprost is believed to raise aqueous humour outflow through the trabecular meshwork and uveoscleral routes [9]. Wikipedia notes that, unlike other prostaglandin analogues, it does not act on the prostaglandin F receptor and is thought to mimic prostamides, for which no receptor had been identified as of 2015 [1]. Reviews of the pharmacology are available [22][23].

For lashes, the proposed explanation is that it prolongs the anagen growth phase and increases the proportion of follicles in that phase, possibly with effects on pigmentation; a laboratory study examined the mechanism of bimatoprost-induced eyelash growth [2][24]. Wikipedia also notes that the drug and its endogenous analogue have anti-adipogenic effects in laboratory work [1].

Bimatoprost is well absorbed through the cornea and starts lowering eye pressure around four hours after application, lasting at least 24 hours. Little reaches the bloodstream, with peak plasma levels at about 10 minutes and levels falling below detection by about 1.5 hours. Plasma protein binding is about 88 percent and half-life after intravenous infusion about 45 minutes [1].

Grokipedia reports that Allergan developed bimatoprost in the early 1990s under the code AGN 192024, filed a patent in 1992, received US Patent 5,688,819 on 18 November 1997, and began clinical trials in 1998 [2]. It sits in a class that began with a 1977 paper showing prostaglandin F2-alpha lowers eye pressure, which led to latanoprost (approved 1996), bimatoprost and travoprost (2001) and tafluprost (2012) [36].

Lumigan 0.03% was approved by the FDA on 16 March 2001 and authorised in the EU on 8 March 2002, with Australia, Canada and Japan following, according to Grokipedia [2]. Increased lash growth was noted as a side effect in glaucoma patients, which led to development for hypotrichosis and FDA approval of Latisse in December 2008 [2]; Wikipedia reports Allergan introduced Latisse in 2009 [35]. The 0.01% Lumigan approval in 2010 added stronger warnings about possibly permanent iris pigmentation [2].

Generic ophthalmic versions entered the US market from late 2014 to 2015, and a sustained-release intracameral implant, Durysta, was approved in 2020 [2]. Grokipedia also reports a preservative-free 0.01% gel from Thea Pharma approved in September 2025 [2]. Allergan was acquired by AbbVie in a deal announced in June 2019 and completed on 8 May 2020 [37]. Wikipedia reports more than 1 million US prescriptions in 2023 [1], and Grokipedia reports about 1.49 million with a peak above 3.4 million in 2020 [2].

A 2024 review states that US law does not require efficacy or safety assessment of over-the-counter eyelash serums before sale, and that some products contain prostaglandin analogues [8]. Latisse is the only FDA-approved drug for increasing lash length, thickness and darkness, per Grokipedia [2].

Wikipedia lists brand names including Lumigan, Careprost, Latisse, Eyreida, Mylash, Zimed, Zolymbus and Visuplain [1]. Careprost is described by Grokipedia as a common Indian generic at 0.03 percent [2]. Grokipedia gives 2025 US prices of about $14 to $80 per month for generic glaucoma bimatoprost, about $270 to $350 for branded Lumigan without insurance, and about $140 to $215 for a Latisse kit, noting that cosmetic use is generally not covered by insurance [2]. Wikipedia lists the drug as prescription-only in the US and EU and Schedule 4 in Australia [1].

On looksmax.org, lashes are treated as an important feature of eye area and eye aesthetics, and Latisse is a recurring topic. One user calls it the best soft-maxxing step he has taken, citing low cost, ease and rare side effects, and says his lashes now curl naturally [28]. Other threads report results after six weeks, describe twitching as a drawback, ask whether to use it, and share guides to using it with fewer side effects [32][33][41][43].

Access is a theme: users in countries where Latisse is unavailable ask about Careprost, with replies saying both contain the same drug [30]. Others ask where to obtain it, whether alternatives exist, and what to use instead, including oral minoxidil [38][40][42]. A recurring concern is the effect on the fat around the eye, with some users saying they avoid it because it burns upper eyelid fat, and others discussing bimatoprost with dermastamping for monolid reshaping [29][31][34].
Research directions include sustained-release implants and inserts for glaucoma [14][25][26][27], and investigational uses in hair loss and anti-adipogenic effects [1][17].

A long-term safety extension of the intracameral implant (ARTEMIS, NCT03891446) is reported by Grokipedia as estimated to finish in August 2026 [2]. The 2024 review notes the ARTEMIS studies found significant implant biodegradation in most of 372 eyes after one year [5].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org bimatoprost, usually under the brand name Latisse, is discussed as an eyelash treatment, with threads on application, side effects, eye colour change, import brands such as Careprost, and fat loss around the eyes [28][29][30][31].

claims.claim: Latisse grows longer, curlier lashes with few side effects.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org user says it is cheap and easy to apply with rare side effects and that his lashes now curl naturally; other threads are titled '6 weeks latisse success' and 'latisse works but be aware of eye twitching' [28][32][33].
claims.experts: In the phase III trials summarised by Grokipedia, nightly use for 16 weeks increased lash length by about 25 percent versus vehicle [2]. The US label reports conjunctival hyperemia as the most common reaction (45 percent) and lists itching, burning and blurred vision [9].

claims.claim: Latisse can change eye colour, a concern for users with light eyes.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster with hazel or light green eyes asks whether anyone used it on the lower lid without noticing a colour change and says users on Reddit fearmonger about side effects [29].
claims.experts: The US label warns of pigmentation of the iris, eyelid tissue and lashes, and says iris pigmentation is likely to be permanent while lash changes are usually reversible [9].

claims.claim: Bimatoprost reduces fat around the eye, which can reshape the eyelid.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread says it removed monolids through bimatoprost with dermastamping, and others discuss whether it works as a fat dissolver; one user says he avoids it because it burns upper eyelid fat [31][34][29].
claims.experts: Grokipedia lists periorbital fat atrophy among reported effects, Wikipedia notes anti-adipogenic effects in laboratory work, and the label warns of periorbital tissue pigmentation [2][1][9]. No trials of bimatoprost for eyelid reshaping exist.

claims.claim: Careprost is the same drug as Latisse.
claims.believers: In a looksmax.org thread a user whose country restricts Latisse asks about Careprost; a reply says both contain the same drug, though the poster wonders whether Latisse has an enhancer [30].
claims.experts: A 2024 review states that US law does not require efficacy or safety assessment of over-the-counter eyelash serums and that some contain prostaglandin analogues [8].

claims.claim: Latisse works on the lower lashes and eyebrows too.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster says he tried every other way to grow his bottom lashes and wants to use Latisse on the lower lid [29].
claims.experts: The approved regimen is for the upper lid margin [4]; a small placebo-controlled eyebrow study was completed in 2011 and a case report described eyebrow growth after eight months [6][1].

claims.claim: Used carefully, Latisse has minimal or no side effects.
claims.believers: Looksmax.org guides are titled around using it with minimal to no side effects, and one user says side effects are pretty rare [43][28].
claims.experts: Law's review lists itching, redness, irritation, dry eye symptoms and eyelid darkening in the lash trial [4], and the label lists hyperemia, pigmentation and other warnings [9].

claims.believers: Threads ask about alternatives when Latisse cannot be obtained, such as one titled about having to use minoxidil instead [38][42].
claims.experts: Law's review states that observable lash growth resolved after stopping latanoprost or bimatoprost [4].

claims.claim: Minoxidil can substitute for Latisse on lashes.
claims.believers: Posters facing access problems discuss oral minoxidil as a fallback and one calls it the only other legit way to grow bottom lashes [42][29].
claims.experts: No published trial located compares minoxidil with bimatoprost for eyelashes.

angle.text: People use bimatoprost on the upper lash line to grow longer, fuller and darker lashes, which changes how defined and open the eyes look without extensions or heavy mascara. Some also apply it to eyebrows, and a few users discuss it for reshaping the area around the eye.
